analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime for police and prison officers to use excessive force or fail to stop it.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in June 2020 with a single cosponsor, died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new federal crime for law enforcement and correctional officers who intentionally or recklessly use more force than is reasonably necessary, causing injury. Intentional acts could carry up to life in prison if someone dies; reckless acts up to 20 years. It would also make it a crime for an officer who watches another officer use excessive force and can stop it to stand by, and it would close the common defense that an officer did not know the force was illegal. The bill went to the House Judiciary Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: People injured or killed by police and correctional officers, and their families, who would gain a federal criminal remedy that does not depend on proving the officer knew the force was unconstitutional. Officers who intervene to stop excessive force also gain, because the law would protect them for stepping in regardless of rank or agency.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People harmed by police and prison officers

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new federal crime (18 U.S.C. § 242A) for officers acting under color of law who cause bodily injury through intentional or reckless use of excessive force, with penalties of up to 10 years for intentional acts and up to life if death results [S3].
Makes it a separate crime for an officer who is aware of ongoing excessive force, has a chance to stop it, and chooses not to intervene, punishable by up to 20 years if death results [S3].
Bars defenses that the officer did not know the specific law or constitutional rule the force violated, and bars junior officers from excusing inaction because the abuser outranked them [S3].
Covers federal, state, and local law enforcement and correctional officers, including contractors, in both street and jail or prison settings [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement and correctional officers and their unions, and the agencies that would face more federal criminal prosecutions and civil friction from a new nationwide use-of-force standard. Taxpayers would fund the additional federal prosecutions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Police and prison officers and their agencies

drawbacks.text: The federal government already has a criminal civil-rights statute (18 U.S.C. § 242) covering excessive force, and federal prosecutions of local officers are rare; critics would argue a new statute adds paperwork without adding real prosecutions, a good-faith objection the bill's narrow support did not answer.
Criminal penalties for recklessness could pressure officers in fast, violent encounters to hesitate rather than act, a cost an honest supporter would have to weigh against the accountability gain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real but narrow: federal criminal accountability for officers whose excessive force injures or kills, plus liability for bystander officers who stand by. The costs are mostly borne by officers facing a new federal exposure and by the justice system, and the bill never got a hearing where these trade-offs could be tested or refined.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in June 2020 and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Adriano Espaillat introduced the bill on June 15, 2020, during a period of national debate over police use of force, and it was referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee [S1].
The bill drew just one cosponsor, a single House Democrat [S4].

The action history shows only two entries: introduction and the committee referral. The Judiciary Committee never reported the bill, and it never came to a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement and correctional officers and their unions are better off, because no new federal excessive-force or failure-to-intervene crime was created; people harmed by police violence are no better off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police and prison officers; no new federal liability

for.name: Rep. Adriano Espaillat
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 15, 2020 and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee.

for.name: 1 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its only cosponsor.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Chair Jerrold Nadler)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 15, 2020 and took no further action; the bill never got a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever recorded, and with a single cosponsor there is no way to tell from the record how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill would expose officers to new federal criminal penalties of up to life in prison for intentional excessive force causing death, up to 20 years for reckless force, and up to 20 years for failing to intervene. Officer unions have generally opposed new criminal liability standards for use of force.

industries.industry: Police departments and prison operators, including private prison contractors
industries.note: Because the bill covers anyone performing a law enforcement or penological function on behalf of any government, including contractors, prison operators' staff would face the same federal exposure as public officers.
